769.t: First seeing a sock cymbal and why full four-beat playing clashes with it
769.s: He first sees a hi-hat around 1930 and argues that for authentic jazz with bass-drum accents it is hard to use.
769.q: Well, the first time I saw a sock cymbal being used was around the year of 1930. That was the first time I seen a muse. That was in New Orleans? Yeah, right here in New Orleans. That was the first time I saw a muse.

769.t: Henry Martin's style and drum set
769.s: Watkins describes Henry Martin's playing, overhanging pedals, cymbal, wood block, snare and a bass drum of about 28 inches.
769.q: Well in them days they had overhanging pedals. Yeah. And he had a cymbal, wood block, in those days they had their wood shell snare drums, and Chinese tum tum. But I never noticed what kind of a drum stand he was using.

769.t: His new drum outfit and the side cymbal on the bass drum
769.s: He bought a $400-500 outfit around 1920-22 and explains the old side-cymbal attachment and why he stays an authentic drummer.
769.q: Well, I don't use all the chaps that the present day drum is used because if you're gonna play authentic, you've got half authentic stuff with you, see? What's the only thing that's missing is the side cymbal on the bass drum.

769.s: Watkins explains why he never bought a hi-hat and that earlier drummers such as Black Benny and Baby Dodds did not use one either.
769.q: No, I never used a hi-hat at no time. No, no. Because see in them days they never used hi-hats. No, no. And it's not necessary for, you use hi-hats and it gives a nice swing, I'll admit to that. It really gives a wonderful swing, but that's alright for these big bands, you understand what I mean?…

769.t: Old pedals and the side cymbal
769.s: Old-time drummers used big bass drums with overhanging pedals and a side cymbal, a technique Watkins learned from watching Baby Dodds.
769.q: They both hit at the same time and then when you want to you just take your stick and just throw it off and wouldn't hear nothing but the bass drum.

769.t: Renting drums and carrying Joe Lynch's snare
769.s: In his youth drum sets could be rented from pawn shops for a dollar a night, and he carried drums to get into dances as Happy did.
769.q: They had a nice volume to them. But I, when I started playing they had to cut out using them. And, well in them days you used to, you was able to go to a pawn shop, we didn't have no drums, you was able to go to a pawn shop and rent a set. Okay. They charge you a dollar for the whole outfit for one…

153.t: Inventing the double bass drum set
153.s: He drew plans in 1938, Ray McKinley and later drummers, and why tap dancing inspired it.
153.q: Well Eddie Shaughnessy came to me once and he said “hey, did you really start the two bass drums? I thought you did, but did Ray McKinley do it first?” I said well I don’t know because when I was a youngster in 1938 I drew the plans for the double bass drum kit. And around 1940, I saw in Down Beat…

153.t: Drawing the double-bass-drum kit in 1938 and the Gretsch prototype
153.s: He sketched the two-bass kit in high school, drum companies thought him crazy, Gretsch built it, and he first used it with FioRito.
153.ch: Double bass drums and the great drummers
153.q: I got the idea in 1938. I was in high school. I made a drawing of the double- bass-drum kit, the one that you see on this [?]. My teacher said, “What are you doing?” I said, “This is a diagram of a new drum set, a new kind of a drum set.” I explained to him that most drummers only use one bass…

153.t: Ray McKinley and who was first with two bass drums
153.s: McKinley told him that Bellson was the first, with McKinley playing two bass drums by mallets in Double Drum Boogie; Bellson believes he was first to add pedals.
153.ch: Double bass drums and the great drummers
153.q: I thought he was the first one, but later on he told me, “No. It was you. You were the first one.” He came up – he was with Will Bradley’s band. Double Drum Boogie came up with him. He had two bass drums, and he played them with mallets. I thought – I kept giving people the idea that Ray was the…

153.t: Engineering the hi-hat to work alongside two bass drums
153.s: He removed the hi-hat tripod and linked it to the bass drum rod, working out a toe-and-heel technique.
153.ch: Double bass drums and the great drummers
153.q: I took the tripod off of the hi-hat and made a connection between the bell of the hi-hat and one of the rods in the bass drum, so that brought it right – this was the bass drum, and the hi-hat was right next to it, by getting rid of the tripod.

153.t: Jingle sticks on the Basie recording
153.s: He explains jingle sticks made from tambourine jingles and Basie's love of them.
153.q: What I did quite a few years ago, I took the jingles off the tambourine and put them on the drum stick. And Basie used to call them bells. “I like those bells — give me those bells” you know he loved that sound. I designed them strictly for maybe bossa novas and Latin things. But then I found out…

153.t: Ambidextrous ideas: extra snares and the silent practice kit
153.s: He recalls other drum inventions, including a rubber practice set he could not patent.
153.ch: Double bass drums and the great drummers
153.q: I knew I was really ambidextrous. I started dreaming about this idea of having another drum on this side. Later on I was the first one to have two snare drums over here and then have an extension of bongo drums over here. So those ideas were coming to me. I was the first one that invented the…

72.t: Early drum kit: 28-inch bass drum, alligator pedal, no hi-hat
72.s: He describes drum boxes, big bass drums, alligator pedals, a single small cymbal, and not knowing hi-hats until New York.
72.q: Well, they didn't use no... They used them... there were drum covers. That's going back as far as Texas Joe(?), had a thing called a... They used to have a box made especially for your drums...

72.s: Early heads were calfskin sold unmounted; Moore describes taping and tucking heads onto the rim himself.
72.q: You had to get your... Say you busted your drumhead. I could put tape on a damaged head, and it would have that sound; it would hold it together, you know. And I used to take a spoon, the end of a spoon, and I used to tuck

72.t: Cozy Cole's 24-inch cymbal and big bass drums
72.s: Cole gave him a 24-inch crash cymbal; Moore recalls huge bass drums, Zutty Singleton's and the show drummer Battleaxe's pedal.
72.q: And they had some very good drummers during that time, very good. Cozy Cole was a great tom-tom man. He loved to play tom-toms. He liked to play cymbals, too. In fact, he gave me a cymbal that was too large for him because he...

72.t: Drumstick types, woods and prices, then and now
72.s: Compares old military sticks with modern plastic-tipped ones; pine, maple and hickory; price per pair; early lack of wire brushes.
72.q: Yeah, military drums. They didn't use the kind of sticks that we use now. In fact, they didn't make them. What they use now is the plastic tips...

72.t: Cymbal and drum makers: Turkish, Zildjian, Ludwig, Slingerland
72.s: Moore moved from Turkish cymbals to Zildjians and uses Ludwig drums.
72.q: Zildjian was kind of expensive. I couldn't get up all that money to get them Zildjians until later on. The Turkish cymbal, which had a nice sound, but it had a loud, harsh sound which was very thick. And there's another cymbal between the Turkish and the Zildjian that had a nice sound. But the…

72.s: Some drummers made their own sticks from limbs with resin; modern sticks warp and are tested on a counter.
72.q: No, there's such a thing as... Some guys used to try to make their sticks. They'd out in the woods, pick up some limbs from the trees the size of the drumsticks, what looked like the size of the drumsticks. They used to whittle them down to the end and take the pine off...the sap off the…

98.s: Cymbals were small and thick in 1934, and both men used heavy brass cymbals as bottom hi-hats.
98.ch: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
98.q: Right, well, that was about the biggest thing you could get at that time. And then they used to have those old thick cymbals, so thick until -- they were almost like a gong.

98.t: The first sock cymbal and the old low hat
98.s: Sitting in at the sessions he saw the first sock cymbal on the floor; DeMichael recalls his own old low hat.
98.q: Right, and it had a thing like a (unintelligible), and then you put your foot on the wood and then a spring, (laughter.)

98.t: Baby Dodds, the low hat and Ludwig and Slingerland
98.s: They talk about Baby Dodds never using a sock cymbal and a story about Ludwig making him a foot cymbal.
98.ch: Big band, Chicago players, recordings and gospel
98.q: Old Man, right, they were always inventing something, they were very instrumental in a lot of new contraptions for drums.

98.t: When ride cymbals and the high hat came in
98.s: Saunders dates the lowboy to 1932 and high hat soon after; early drummers like Dodds, Singleton and Krupa used snare shimmy beats instead of ride cymbals.
98.ch: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
98.q: Well, like I told you earlier, we talked about it. Now, in 1932, that was -- there was a lowboy, see, and right after that, I would say, between 1932 and 1935, they started coming out with --

98.t: How drums have changed: heads, toms, cymbals and his own setup
98.s: Drum heads went from cowhide to plastic and kits grew to ten toms and two bass drums; Saunders keeps two toms and two cymbals.
98.ch: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
98.q: Yeah, the heads changed from the cowhide and then they went into the plastic and all of that, and then years ago they had a rope across and you pulled this --

999.t: Tambourine and sock cymbals on early kits
999.s: They discuss the clamped-on tambourine and the low sock cymbal of early days.
999.ch: Other drummers and New Orleans musicians
999.q: Well they used that just like a, looked like a tum tum too, you know, just hit licks on it. It's not. Hold it up in one hand or have it down? No, no, they had it, some kind of way they had it clamped on the side of the bass.

999.s: He and Allen discuss the old kits: overhead cymbal, tom-tom, tambourine, whistle, ratchet and wood blocks.
999.ch: Early drum sets and dance-hall era
999.q: foot pedal, snare, a bass drum, and what else? Well they had this, I don't know what you call it, a chani, something, a chani name of tom-toms they had. The guys had several of these, a tambourine used to hook up and use that too.

999.s: The cymbal was mounted on the bass drum and sometimes struck with a coat-hanger rim.
999.ch: Other drummers and New Orleans musicians
999.q: And what did he hit it with? Well a lot of times we made a, just taking a coat hanger off, a piece of white and made a rim.

999.s: He names big-band drummers Sidney Montague and Stanley, the Sonny South orchestra, and his neighbor Professor Shalla Neal.
999.ch: Early drum sets and dance-hall era
999.q: Well I do know Sidney Montague, the drummer, and let's see who else. Stanley, well those guys was playing in the big bands. What are you used to do with that big band? Now this guy, Alfred Martin, I think he used to name.

49.t: The first foot pedal and Emil Gonzalez the drum repairman
49.s: Hazel describes the earliest bass drum foot pedal in detail and recommends Emil Gonzalez, a drum mechanic and collector who might still have one.
49.q: I can't remember when, the date, but I can describe it to you. It had a long metal rod. And on the end of the rod was the beater. And then there was a, in the end of the beater, there was a little screw thing that was sort of a, triangle in shape. And you fit a leather strap through that. And you…

49.t: Wood blocks, tom-toms and the old Chinese crash cymbal
49.s: He describes the percussion accessories used in jazz and the 22-inch Chinese crash cymbal he used on early records, later stolen.
49.q: Yeah, the old Chinese. And, uh, and the, the, the, the old Chinese crash was always, for jazz, was always a thing. And then later on, they came out with the Sildjans. And, uh, I never did stop using the crash. And, uh, the, then later on, they put the rivets in the, in the, the old Chinese crash,…

49.t: Double drums, early traps and the first hi-hat
49.s: He explains that double drums meant two men, describes cymbal attachments on the foot pedal, and credits Ray Bauduc with the first low hi-hat.
49.q: Well, instead of having one man play both drums, you know, with the foot pedal and that, well, you had, you had two men. One played the bass drum and one played the snare drum. Not only in parades, now this was for any, any, any dances at all. Because there was no such thing as the foot pedal there.

49.t: Bass drum sizes for dances and parades
49.s: He gives typical bass drum sizes, his own 16 by 30, and the narrower drums colored parade drummers used.
49.q: big drums or smaller drums? Well for the dance jobs they used the bigger drums. They ran anywhere from 12 inches to 16. I had a 16 by 30. About 30 inches and really a big drum. And 16 inches wide. But the standard was the 1428. But for parades, some of the guys used to use these little narrow…

306.t: When the sock cymbal came in and the drumming on the Kid Rena record
306.s: Rene dates the sock cymbal to about 1928-30. They note the record is mostly snare and bass, and Rene thinks he may have left the sock off.
306.ch: Louis Armstrong picture, Kid Rena record and Bunk
306.q: Oh, the sock cymbal come in here somewhere around, I believe, in 29, 30 or 28 or something like that. Like that. It went big, though.

306.t: Rene's drum set: snare, cymbal, tom-toms and traps
306.s: Zander asks about snare, make, crash cymbal, Chinese tom-toms, woodblock and cowbells; Rene mentions his brother and Louis Armstrong drawing a crowd.
306.q: I used one crash cymbal. Chinese? Chinese crash cymbal. And hit it wide open. Oh man, the drummer was a noisy thing. And the people liked that noise, you know? And another thing too, again, in the days like that, it looked like the lollier play, a lot of people like it. Like that Mr. Clot Miller,…

306.t: Bass drum size, swinging pedals and foot technique
306.s: He describes his 32-inch bass drum, its carrying power, and how the swinging pedals were played with the leg kicking wide open.
306.q: Well then the bass drum, you could actually, if the wind was blowing this way, and it would be at night when things were solid or solid, you could actually hear my bass drum at least a mile. Well I'll tell you to prove that fact, we used to play at the Bulls Club. And they said, yeah, my brother,…

306.s: Rene offers to show a ratchet stick, which he says people copied for the market.
306.q: Oh, yeah. A ratchet stick. I can show you. You know, knife. I said, you have a knife. I can show you at the end of this table with a ratchet stick. They actually had them on the market. They came out of the market. You know, at that time, there used to be fellas, I noticed, there used to be fellas…

246.t: Tin flutes and old drum equipment
246.s: Prices of tin flutes and Glass's old drum gear: car bells, triangles, temple blocks and tum-tums.
246.ch: Bands, lake camps and early players
246.q: Ten cents. Ten cents. When you get a big one, they charge you fifty cents for a big one. They find out they were playing music with. They charge you fifty cents. I have a flute home where we used to play in the band. It's plastic. I got one of the plastic. I got it home. I got all my skulls home…

246.t: Early band sizes and the strap bass drum pedal
246.s: Glass describes four-piece bands, two drums, and the old strap foot pedal for the bass drum.
246.q: Two drums. Bass drums. We had our drums, we had a strap, our pedal, our foot pedal was a strap that come from over here. See, you'd press down on it and hit that bass drum with that strap and it had a big ball on the middle there. See, you'd pull that strap.

246.t: The wire beater for the cymbal and two-handed bass drumming
246.s: Glass credits Black Benny with the cymbal beater, says he made one, and compares it with two-handed school band drumming.
246.q: Did they have anything like that? No, some of them didn't. I never seen them with it. But they started using it now, you know? Because that answers for the music, you have to have that cymbal, that brass. Some of the other bands, they'd have two cymbals. They'd have a band, they'd have them two…

922.t: Father's sticks and perforated duplex snare drum
922.s: Light number-five sticks, snare on the street, and the nickel and brass perforated duplex snares, one now owned by Lester.
922.q: Well, he did, but he had on the last, he was using a duplex out on the street. It was a duplex snare drum. I think Lester San Diego had one of the models of the one that he had. I think Lester has it now.

922.t: The collapsible bass drum from New York
922.s: The folding two-head metal bass drum his father got in New York in 1923; Sonny Greer had one too.
922.q: The latest set that he had was a leaded. I can remember the latest set that he had was a leaded. Now, the set right before the leaded was a collapsible set that he had. He got that when he had gone to New York in 23 with the Pierron's band. It was the folding bass drum. When it would collapse, you…

922.t: Father's percussion effects, slapstick and snare 'holler'
922.s: He used bells, wood block, cymbals, whistles, ratchet and slapstick, and an effect of blowing on the snare.
922.q: He used all those. I can remember with orchestra bells, I can remember with the triangle, I can remember with the wood block, the crash cymbal. The other cymbal that they used to place on the bass drum, also with a spar. And they would hit the bass drum and the cymbal on the side for an effect at…

957.t: His first drum outfit and early single-head drums
957.s: He describes his first set: 14x26 bass drum, double-head snare, and the single-head gut-snare drums of Mac Murray and John Veen, with rope or key tensioning.
957.q: See, those keys was made different. They were made on the order, but not the same thing. Because those keys that they had at that time, you could open a water faucet with them. They were all together. They were much larger.

957.t: Foot pedal, cymbals and tom-tom of the early kit
957.s: He recalls the crow-foot pedal, the Chinese and side cymbals, and the single small tom-tom, and says he can still make modern effects on the old kit.
957.q: They were made on the order, the flow pedals of today, but they were much larger, and they had wood balls on them. And we used to use the cymbal on the side of the drum. You know, the drum and the cymbal would beat together, just like they had an old-time electric piano.

957.s: His outfit included four cowbells and a set of four china or temple blocks.
957.q: But we so used to call them the single blocks, you know, the regular china blocks that we call them.

865.t: His first drum set and the overhead beater
865.s: He liked drums best; his first was a tuxedo set with a large bass drum and an overhead beater, which he kept until Chicago.
865.q: Yeah, it was a big bass drum. It was a very big bass drum. You got a big one in the back. I got a big one in the back. Oh yeah, a big 28 inch or something. Yeah, 28. This is a 14 by 22. It was one just like this. It had a single extension on it you see. It didn't have the double. It didn't make the…

865.t: Mechanism details, the Slingerland make, and the stolen trap
865.s: He answers questions on the strap, wooden pedal and packing of the overhead trap, names Slingerland as maker, and tells how it was stolen.
865.q: They had a, they had a, in the back of the ball, you see, they had a little hook, you see, and this foot pedal here would come up, you see, that strap would come up and hook that beater, you see.

865.t: Keeping his drums spotless; parade drum and cymbals
865.s: Phillips keeps many sets and cleans them after jobs. The group admires his parade drum and hand-made beaters.
865.q: Clean my drum. I take my bed and then I go to bed. I'm going to put them on bed. And I just keep them all in good condition. For the person to come for me to play that. It's all hooked up. That's my parade drum back there. That's a little bit of one back there. Right in the back of the door.

997.t: His first set of drums from Paul
997.s: The first set was a single-tension light mahogany set from Grunewald with a 14 by 28 bass drum and Chinese cymbals.
997.q: well yeah that that was uh Levy Levy yeah that was bought at at Grunwald here when they were on Canal Street canal between Boeben and Aurora 700 blocks 733 canal that's what all that my dad bought him that

997.s: He describes a drummer's collapsible duplex drum set that folded into one case.
997.q: I just don't know. Wooden must have some kind of a wood to it. You understand what I mean? To fold.

997.t: Later drum sets and sizes, modern drummers
997.s: He has owned about five sets, shrinking bass drums from 28 to 22, and discusses small drums and progressive drummers like Ed Blackwell.
997.q: well just to get old and you just want to change about that time's got modern you want to keep up with the time that's all

224.t: The first Paiste flat ride cymbal
224.s: He got one of the first Paiste flat rides in Europe and believes it was first recorded on Now He Sings, Now He Sobs.
224.q: Yeah, they had given it to me there. It’s somewhere in Europe, if I remember correctly.

224.t: Getting Ludwig drums in Chicago and switching to Slingerland
224.s: Max Roach led him to the Ludwig factory, he got a 20-inch bass drum, then left Ludwig for Slingerland after a snub.
224.q: with him. Charlie carries on there. I don’t know. A whole long – anyhow, Charlie gets fired. In the meantime, I think Howard McGhee goes in there. So meantime, Max and Miles were still in town, half stranded. I think they got back through the union or something. In the meantime, they’re all at this…

224.t: Ludwig after the Beatles, and the Pittsburgh hall of fame
224.s: Ludwig's vice president celebrated Ringo's boost and welcomed him back as the first endorser to return; he was inducted into the University of Pittsburgh hall of fame in 1994.
224.q: Ringo. Ludwig says – I’m sitting in Ludwig’s office. Ludwig – now that I’m getting popular again. I’m sitting with the vice president. He really wanted to be the president. He’s in his sixties. His father’s in his nineties. He’s waiting to be president. His father won’t die. That’s the only way he…

26.t: Drum kit before 1930 and the first sock cymbals
26.s: Greer describes his early drum set and the wooden foot-clappers that preceded the high-hat.
26.ch: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
26.q: Now, at that time, let's just fill in, before we go on because now we're up to the Cotton Club, but what kind of equipment had you used before then? I got photographs of you -- hold it a moment. (Recording interruption) Bass drum, snare drum, high hat, two tom toms, two 16-inch tom toms on the…

26.t: Designing drums for the Leedy factory
26.s: A company executive hires Greer as drum designer; five trunks of gleaming drums arrive and impress the gangsters.
26.ch: New York, the Kentucky Club and the high-hat
26.q: That's when I started. A fellow, one of the executives of the club come to New York and seen me playing at the Kentucky Club. He said, 'Sonny, how would you like to work for us?' I said, 'What doing?' He said, 'designing, and using all our advance products.' I said, 'all right.' I say, 'well, send…

26.t: Staged fires at the Kentucky Club and the gold cymbal
26.s: The boss arranged fires when business was slack; Greer polished smoked cymbals and sold one to a California Ramblers drummer.
26.ch: The Washingtonians, Bechet and drum style
26.q: I had a cymbal -- They had a band called the California Ramblers, a big white band, and the drummer was Stanley somebody. They were a good band, they could play, big band, so we had a fire. That was the ritual--the fire, when a holiday come up like the -- what's that day -- Palm Sunday or…

147.t: Sock cymbals and Kaiser Marshall's high hat
147.s: Crawford describes the flat floor sock cymbal and says Kaiser Marshall was the first he saw play a high hat.
147.ch: Learning the drums and early influences
147.q: Well, I think he brought them out. I, you know, I think he brought them out, high hat cymbal.

147.t: The first drum set and playing the back beat
147.s: Crawford and Crouch reconstruct his first set of bass drum, snare and small sock cymbal, played on two and four.
147.ch: Learning the drums and early influences
147.q: That you had to put your foot through a strap to maintain it steady and go up and down with it.

147.t: Sonny Greer's equipment and Gene Krupa's tympani
147.s: Crouch and Crawford discuss how Greer's big set-up inspired other drummers to collect equipment.
147.ch: Heroes, rivals and the drummers' craft

384.s: He explains naming his tuned drums N'goma from a dictionary, how they were built and tuned with a key, and that they led to his being offered a band.
384.ch: Hutto 1978-79: NBC, radio and the N'goma drums
384.q: Yes and I got that out of a dictionary. And I went through all the drums in the dictionary to find out what the hell to call these things. And this was a

384.t: 1939 article: his collection of exotic drums
384.s: The article describes drums from Turkey, Cuba, China, Haiti and Indo-China, many used as radio sound effects.
384.ch: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings
384.q: foreign drums, he is rapidly becoming one. He admits that although it didn't start as a hobby, his collection is proving so engrossing, it is rapidly becoming one. Piece by piece, he has collected an unusual set of drums from foreign countries. One of them is a clay drum shaped like a vase from…

384.s: A 1939 Long Island Daily Press article describes his 14 drums tuned from B flat to B flat, his film short with Leith Stevens, and recordings of Mazi-Pani and Ku-li-a.
384.ch: N'goma drums and the scrapbook clippings
384.q: Daily Press, Saturday, March 25, 1939. Obviously that other article from the newspaper called the Press is the same one, the same newspaper, Long Island Daily Press. This one is entitled "Chauncey Morehouse of Forest Hills collects Weird Drums". The subtitle is - has 14 tuned to different pitches…

241.s: He bought a slapstick after seeing one in a shop, as old-time drummers used them, and says the one Russell made of oak flooring snaps better.
241.q: He said, that's a slapstick. I bought it, you know? Oh, Mr. Bill, that must have been wrong when in the 30s. The old time drummers used to use them.

241.t: Sam Morgan's band, drummers' gadgets and the triangle
241.s: Sam Morgan's drummer used a slapstick; Valentine recalls vaudeville drummers' gadgets such as whistles and sandpaper blocks and the triangle.

248.t: Drums, big dance halls and sailors' tips
248.s: Drums were standard; Hunts and Nagle and the 101 Ranch drew Norwegian sailors whose tips included gold pieces.
248.ch: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
248.q: Oh, practically most all the bands had drums. Oh, they did have drums? Yeah, that was the main instrument, a drum. Piano and drum, they always had that. Oh, did they? Yeah, they never did, they'd be without that drum. Oh. Out of all the time when they didn't have no blowing instruments, they used…

248.t: Old-time cymbals, cow bells, ice cream bells, triangles and brushes
248.s: Dawson describes the percussion drummers used: small cymbals, cow bells, bell sets, iron triangles, and straw brushes for soft music.
248.q: Then the cymbals, uh, well, uh, had, uh, the old-time cymbals. Didn't have all these cymbals like they got now. Oh. Had one, two, little small cymbals, and they had what you call a, uh, bells. Yeah. A bell, like, like, oh, a cow bell. Mm-hmm. And, uh, you know, a cow bell. They had different,…

177.t: His father's homemade drum set and what became of it
177.s: Describes his father's wooden trap pedal, Chinese cymbals, blocks and cowbells; his mother got rid of the set and he later bought his own.
177.q: He didn't have an overhead foot pedal. He had one made in a trap form because it's different in foot pedals. And an overhead foot pedal and a trap foot pedal was made out of wood. But these days they are made out of iron, but they're traps. Yeah. But in those days they were considered as overhead…

177.t: Father's homemade foot pedal and two-drum trap set
177.s: Father built a wooden foot pedal and played two drums together, but one drum in parades.
177.q: It was an overhead foot pedal at that time. That's the only kind they had. And they was called overhead. And he made himself a foot pedal out of wood.

871.t: Drum set on the advertising trucks
871.s: The drum set he used on the trucks had an overhead foot pedal, one cymbal and a woodblock, and he sat at the front of the truck.
871.q: That's right. You see, we didn't have no big tum tum or nothing like that. We just had them little bit of tum tum on the side of a wood block and one cymbal, and that overhead pedal. And you'd snag drum, and you'd stand, that's it.

871.t: Stolen cymbals, sock cymbal and an old pedal
871.s: His cymbals were stolen at the American Legion Hall; he talks about cowbell, wood block and wanting an old foot pedal.
871.q: That's the sizzle, I call it a sizzle symbol sometimes, don't they? Right, right. It's like little rivets in there, isn't it? Yeah. Yeah, about a dozen, there are about eight little rivets in there. That's the turn. Let's see what make that is. That's a nice Turkish one, sounds good. I was…

430.t: Early drum sets: banjo-shell snare, rope bass drums, pedals and cymbals
430.s: Details of the snare, bass drum ropes and pedals, tom-toms, Chinese cymbals and wood blocks used by early New Orleans drummers.
430.q: That's what he had, that's right, real banjo, that's right. Really? That's what he had, that's right, real banjo, that's right. That's right, I'm not, I'm not, I'm telling you something I seen with these two.

430.t: Cymbal use and the going-out chorus
430.s: Crash cymbal was used on the out chorus, volume rising, and choked or left ringing.
430.q: Well, they'd just use a cymbal for going out, you know. We call it on the Gone Out Chorus, you know, on the Gone Out Chorus. We'd use it then, see.

827.t: Father's nickel-plated snare drum and its loss
827.s: Father played only drums; his nickel-plated snare, bought from a ship's man, was left to Arthur but his cousin lost it.
827.q: And I had a cousin, was playing drum at the time, and I was so small I wasn't worrying with it then. My cousin borrowed him from me, never to give him back to me. Now he's a kiddle drum, it came from France. He bought it from a fellow off the ship from France.

827.t: Details of father's drum kit, sticks and brushes
827.s: Arthur describes the wood block, cymbal and pedal setup, and says no wire brushes were used then.
827.q: Well, he had a wood box, I can remember that well, because I watched him play. He had a wood box, he had those cymbals hang, you know, that you beat on it. He had one on the side of the drum. The pedal hit. Yeah, the pedal hit. I can remember that set of drums well. I remember that he did have that…

634.t: Drum makes, pedals, cymbals and 5A sticks
634.s: He liked a Leedy snare and Ludwig bass drum, describes the old overhead pedals, cymbals hooked to the bass drum, and medium 5A sticks like Chandler and Cantrell used.
634.q: Well, at that time, years ago, they used to use them overhead pedals. Well, see, they never had those short pedals out yet. You know, they just had them overhead pedals, or a rod on it about that long, and a ball at it. And the pedal part was made out of wood set on the floor with a spring on it.…

634.t: Wood blocks, car bells, temple blocks and Joe Sprott
634.s: When wood blocks and car bells were used, temple blocks, and Joe Sprott as the best on them.
634.q: And when they were using car bells, you know when they had car bells. Yeah. The four car bells. Mm-hmm. Well, that was on the music too. And I used to play a hell of a car bells. Make a kangaroo noise.

184.t: His first drum set, bass drum and foot pedal
184.s: Hall describes his first outfit with snare, one cymbal, cowbell and wood block, rope-tension bass drums, gut snares and the early wooden pedal.
184.ch: Drum sets and New Orleans drummers
184.q: Yeah, the first one he gave me, that time I had a wooden drum. I had a snare drum, pretty good size, I forget how big it was. And all kind of a make up set, you know. One cymbal and one cowbell. And at that days they wasn't used a hi-hat cymbal then. The cymbal was on the side of the drum, yeah,…

184.t: Hi-hat, Chinese cymbal and the Firehouse Five Plus Two
184.s: Hall describes adopting the hi-hat, his old Chinese cymbal, and his friendship with Ward Kimball and Disney players who jammed at his home.
184.q: Nothing proved it. I believe it. And now we did, they had a little band, and on a Sunday afternoon after we met them, my wife and all, we used to go out here and he lives in St. Gable. We used to go out there and make a big pot of gumbo and he'd get a big tub of soda water and beer, and we'd jam…

829.t: How cymbals were mounted on the bass drum over time
829.s: Robertson describes the old practice of carrying a cymbal in the hand, later replaced by a mounted cymbal with a beater, because the old way made too much noise.
829.q: See, they made a beater like that. Well, that's the difference in that it's just like a sock cymbal. Now that's the difference in that flam, it made too much of noise. Yeah. It made too much of noise and it slapped.

829.t: Preferring snare drum; his own beat and snare drum
829.s: Robertson says he would rather play snare drum but is always asked for bass drum, describes his own snare beat and his wooden snare drum.
829.q: I liked it that better than I did bass drum. Oh, you did, huh? Yeah, but they don't let me play no snare drum. Every time they want me on bass drum, they don't want somebody else on snare drum. And I'd rather play snare drum than play bass drum. I'd get the kick out of playing snare drum, but…

847.t: Wearing out the old set, buying from Hall Drum
847.s: The pawn shop set was worn out with Sidney; he now uses a set bought from Hall Drum Company.
847.q: I don't have the set of drums. I have another set. I bought another set from Hall, about four years ago. About four or five years ago. From Hall Drum Shop. Oh. I got a wonderful set in there and I bought from Hall Drums. The drums. The drums I had Sydney. I just wore them at the time. I just wore…

847.t: Cowbells and temple blocks, then and now
847.s: Old drummers had three or four tuned cowbells mounted on the drum; today's use one, more modernistically.
847.ch: Drum sets, small bands and the depression
847.q: Yeah, well they're different in cowbells now. You use them more modernistic. Even when you're playing Dixieland, you don't beat them as much as you used to do. Sometimes guys just take two sticks, you know, just take two sticks and stay on a cowbell. Maybe all through a number, all through a curve.…

880.t: The Ory band's instruments: drum set-up, valve trombone, first slide
880.s: Joseph and Allen discuss the dead drummer, bass drum with crowfoot pedal and side cymbal, homemade traps and hitting the rim instead of wood blocks. Ory's trombone was a valve trombone; Henry Sawyer was the first man Joseph saw with a slide.
880.q: Drummer's dead. Drummer. Drummer. Drummer. Yeah drummer. Good. He's a good drummer. After he got down here and got him a little good drummer. He was some drummer. Drummer. Mm-hmm. Drummer. Mm-hmm. Drummer. Mm-hmm.

880.t: Drum pedal and use of Derby mutes in the picture
880.s: The men examine the crowfoot pedal and what is in the grass by Ory's foot, and Joseph says the only mute used then was the derby.
880.q: Oh, yes. Just something holding that drum, that's all. Holding that drum on the sides, you know? Mmhmm. Just something holding that drum up. That's all? Yeah. Yeah. Sure.

192.t: When Cottrell used the folding drum; his cymbals and snare
192.s: Around 1923-25 with the Piron band; Frazier recalls Zildjian cymbals and a four-inch shell snare.
192.q: That year, yeah. I remember that. That was around in, let's see, 23, 23. I was thinking about around 1925 like that. Yeah.

192.t: Frazier's parade drums and present snare, bass drum and cymbal
192.s: He recalls the duplex snare shared with Alfred Williams, describes his current Leedy snare, Slingerland bass drum, price paid in 1947 and Zildjian cymbal.
192.q: Well, not this snare drum. I had another black. They both live. I had a black wood shell drum, similar to one like Happy Youth. And lots of parades in the later years, I used to use the same drum on his trapania used. Used to call it duplex snare drum. Oh, duplex. Me and Alfred used to alternate…

766.t: His first drum set and the old wooden equipment
766.s: The first set had a narrow two-headed bass drum and a wooden snare and pedal; he later bought a new set.
766.q: New set, I got a whole new, yeah, I got that new set I bought from Coins. That's what the set I bought from Coins. Oh, I see.

766.t: His present drums and big bass drum
766.s: He plays Ludwig and has had about three sets; he prefers his large 14 by 28 bass drum.
766.q: I get off every day at twelve o'clock. What kind of a set of drums are you playing now? What makes you better? I don't know. I don't know.

471.s: Cobb discusses cymbals and the theft in Madrid.
471.ch: Bookie's studio, bands and downtown clubs
471.q: Not most. It’s very important, but not the most important. The drum kit is a good thing too. You have to have a good drum kit, and you have to have good cymbals. In fact, I just had the best cymbals I ever had, stolen in Madrid, this last trip, the ones that I finally got comfortable with, that I…

471.s: Marshall Fisher's car was robbed of the drum set, replaced by Pearl.
471.ch: Bookie's studio, bands and downtown clubs
471.q: Nah, he just wanted to invite us to his house and party. I said, no way I’m going to do that with you, man. That was really some dirty stuff he did. I guess he was on a shoestring. I guess he figured that was what he had to do. So that’s how that went down. Bookie’s place was lively. In fact, this…

237.t: His first drum set, a Duplex, bought in Alexandria
237.s: He bought Duplex drums in Alexandria, with swinging pedals and skin heads that stayed sharp; his later set was a Rogers.
237.ch: Learning drums and recording on the Coast
237.q: Yeah, makes no difference how damp the weather is, man, they're still sharp, they still stay sharp. I've never seen nothing like that before.

237.s: Lovett lists Duplex, Leedy and Ludwig drums, plays any sticks, uses 7As, and the two talk brushes.
237.q: I don't have a favorite stick. I play with all of them. If they're light I play with them and if they're heavy I play with them.

76.t: Sleigh bells bought at Connie's Inn in 1929
76.s: The sleigh bells in the case were bought in 1929 for a Christmas show at Connie's Inn, when Hal Baquet played Santa Claus. Dance remarks on percussion fashions today.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
76.q: For Christmas, Santa, Hal Bacquet (Falcon) was Santa Claus I believe. Big guy, he sure didn't look like Santa Claus. And every now and then Hal would have me come in with the sleigh bells. (SOUND OF BELLS IN BACKGROUND). Well, I bought them in 1929.

76.t: His bag of tricks and how jazz noises came from the theater
76.s: Zutty lists the gong, auto horn and duck call he used in theaters and big bands. He and Dance agree the novelty noises in early jazz came from theater work, not dance halls.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership
76.q: Chinese gong. You see, and I used to use that right in the theater. And when I started playing in big bands well I still used it.

249.t: Old drum equipment: no sock cymbal, rods, crash cymbal
249.s: Early kits had no sock cymbal; an overhead paddle and thin crash cymbals.
249.q: They had no sock cymbal. What kind of cymbals did you use when you started? Well, you understand, we had an overhead paddle, you see. Yeah, on the bass drum. And on your floor, B would hit the cymbal.

179.s: Cottrell, the best drummer, bought drums from a warehouse and used a set that folded into a case.
179.ch: Casimir, Bigard and Allen's brass band
179.q: Well, I think, uh, out of all of them drummers growing, I think Contrell was about the best drummer over there. I never saw him. No, he was tall. He died. He used to, he used to age in for war lines. He never bought no drums. All he done went in. War lines and got him a set of drums and go out…

82.t: Stan King's drumming, early electrical recording, and the goofus
82.s: Acoustic recording could not take bass drums, and Stan King's press roll anchored the rhythm. Kirkeby recounts novelty instruments, Rollini's coenophone and coining the name Goofus Five.
82.q: That's right. We never, I don't believe, even when an electrical recording came, and we made the first electrical session for Columbia in Columbus Circle. And I remarked at the time what a different setup was going to mean in comfort and ease of operation as far as balance and isolation of solo…

899.t: His early drum set: cowbells, cymbals, overhead beater
899.s: He describes his full set with four cowbells, Chinese and Turkish cymbals and the old overhead beater.
899.ch: Learning the drums and first job
899.q: It was an overhead beater we had first. Yeah. You had the overhead beater. Yeah.

255.t: The overhead foot pedal and Dave Biddy's drums
255.s: He describes the old overhead foot pedal with rod and spring, and Dave Biddy as the last man to own one.
255.q: Well, the beat was much different from the day on the ottoman for the drums that we had and the foot pellet was different. Now we had what you call an overhead foot pattern. Yeah. That foot pellet would come over and it had a rod and a spring in the middle and it would kick out on the back. And…

771.s: Bocage describes the aluminum folding bass drum that Cottrell carried and used with the band.
771.q: Lewis, young Lewis, he told me about that. It folded up and went into a little case, well, it wasn't much bigger than that.

258.t: Early drum set, cymbals and traps; a few clarinet lessons
258.s: He describes his junior set with strap-tuned snare, overhead pedal, cymbals, cowbells and effects, and his short clarinet study.
258.ch: Learning drums and trombone, New Orleans
258.q: Well the first set of drums I had it was a little set you... Well it was a small set. It was a junior set and the traps consist of bass drum, snare drum. And the snare drum I used to tune it up with straps. Didn't have any screws on it. Oh yeah.

260.t: Ray's Chinese cymbal and the sizzle cymbal with Zildjian
260.s: Ray had Avedis Zildjian design a sizzle cymbal with rivets when Chinese cymbals could not be had because of the war between China and Japan.
260.q: Well, we got the new sizzle cymbal that we worked out with Mr. Bedeus Zildjian. It came about during the time of the Chinese war, the Chinese war with Japan.

626.t: Drums and basses in the early string bands
626.s: He explains that early string bands had bass violins and later a trap drum played by one man.
626.ch: Church, Creole life and Mobile musicians
626.q: Well, they'd have a, they'd have a, what they call a, they'd have a drum with a cymbal on it and a trap. They'd call it a trap drum, you see. Now one man would use both. He'd use his foot with the bass drum, it wouldn't be very loud, you see. And he'd use his hand with the snare drum. They had the…

857.t: Cymbals, wood blocks and the drum kit
857.s: Foster describes his German hand-hammered cymbal, a gift, plus his wood block, cowbell, Chinese cymbals, tom-tom and bass drum sizes.
857.q: Because at that time I used to could get a good symbol for $16. That symbol that cost $65. That is a symbol that comes from Germany.

570.t: Early drum kit: pedals, cymbals and no sock cymbal
570.s: Describes his first set, homemade overhead beater and pedal, small cymbals, blocks and cowbells; he never saw a sock cymbal until New Orleans.
570.q: Well it was a good set he bought for me. It was a leaders. Did you? Yes he came down the audience and bought it for me and I still was in Morgan City. And they surprised me one night with a set of drums.

688.t: His drum set, cowbells, and floor pedal technique
688.s: He lists the cymbals, blocks, cowbells and tom-toms he used, prefers the floor pedal, and describes beating with his toes like the drummer Roy.
688.q: I had everything. I work in a cabaret out on Decatur Street. And I had everything. Wood blocks, bells, I got all in here. Cowbells? Yeah. How many of those did you use? Four. Four of them. Four-carter belly, wood blocks. I had triangles. I had two triangles. And two Tom-Toms. And I want to sell an…

572.s: He tells how he moved from Leedy to Ludwig drums and got Zildjian to make a thin splash cymbal to his specification.
572.q: Well, I mean, uh, these guys that trim them down there, they just make a, uh, it was a matter of form. This is a cymbal of certain size. That, that, that's all I worried about. Yeah. You understand? The size of the cymbal, and, and it had to be cut down to certain thickness, and that was it. But…

884.t: His boyhood drum set: rope-tension drums and single-head snare
884.s: Describes rope-tension bass and snare drums, rosin on the ropes, a single head with gut snares, and having only cymbals.
884.q: We had bass drums. They had rope on them. I guess you done seen those. I've seen rounds of kids too, yeah. They have little rubber things like on them. You'd pull them, you'd grease them as rosim, you know, and you'd pull them down, that would tighten it. Yeah.

885.s: They bought raw skins from Old Man Hall's store, soaked them overnight and mounted them.
885.q: Oh yeah, we used to make up, you know, we'd get the loose heads and soak them in water overnight. Oh really? Yeah, it'd sell the, it wouldn't be mounted, you know, it'd be just the skin. Right. Old Man Hall, he used to have a drum store down on Charter Street. He played with the symphony for many…

56.t: Rhythm instruments and the washtub drum
56.s: A wash tub deadened with rags and a foot pedal served as the first drum set.
56.q: Well, the same instrument I had. We had the guitar and the violin and bass. Banjo. And banjo. And the drum. Well, later we had the drums, you see. That came later. Yeah. Taking a big tub and then a foot pedal, you know.

832.t: His first drum set, a Wallace outfit
832.s: Foster tells of his first drum set, a 26-inch bass drum from Wallace that took six months to reach Mandeville, cost about $110 and came with four cowbells.
832.q: He was playing with Buddy, and he was playing with Buddy, and he was playing with Buddy. And I told Buddy I was playing, I had my drums, and he was surprised. I made him on a big Sunday night. I mean, a big Monday night we played at Cheshire Club, and it was Rowley. I was playing with him. He was…

715.s: Allen credits Jasper Taylor, then Floyd Casey, with the washboard; discusses its use on records and in the burlesque show.
715.q: He came in with us with this brother show I was telling you about. And I picked up a band, I picked up the New York with his band, and it seemed like he had did somebody call in or something out there in Chicago and he knew Clarence, so he went to Clarence and talked to everybody. It seemed like.…

308.t: Wire brushes, hi-hat and low boy pedals
308.s: Frazier talks about wire brushes and his first hi-hat in the late 1930s.
308.q: and then you can take your wire brushes on your drum and don't drown them man I'd play soft you know take two sticks of wire brushes when that phrase come on this beat nice and soft and don't drown them out. When did wire brushes come in? Yeah they come in but they've been here wire brushes some…

887.s: The Wild Magnolias are heard; Cahn explains tambourine and cowbell, with few drums since the men march all day.
887.q: Yes. They have the tambourine and the cowbell. The cowbell. That's it, more or less. They have introduced... A couple of tribes have introduced either a bass drum or a type of bongo. Right. Or march bongo. But you have to realize that on Mardi Gras Day, these fellas march from 6 or 7 in the morning…

309.t: Homemade guitar picks and drummer Charlie Blue Watson
309.s: Players cut picks from combs and corset stays; Julius's cousin Charlie Watson drummed for his father.
309.q: Well, at that time, the guitar players used to take the regular combs, you know, that the ladies used to comb their hair with. Well, they had this part, it was about that wide before the comb part. Right. And they used to take a file or a knife and shave it down and then, you know, make picks out…

1034.t: Answering services and the cartage companies
1034.s: Busy session players used answering services, and Hal Blaine and others pioneered drum cartage between studios.
1034.q: Yeah. Well it was so busy back then, everybody had an answering service. And after every session, everybody’d be out in the hall on the — not cell phones — on the pay phones, calling their service to see what dates were booked for them the next day or the next week or that type of thing. And they’d…

105.t: The power of the drum and his book
105.s: Drums stop traffic and draw children; he names his book in progress.
105.q: So see what I mean? And my instrument has been more devastating than bombs. You know to strike the fear into a human being. Hitler proved that when he had this march you know. In the early years of Africa the drums — hey you heard them, boom, boom, right? And the Indians — boom, boom, boom, boom…

354.t: The shared drum cases at the recording studios
354.s: Studio drummers shared locked drum cases left at studios so they could go straight from the Cavett show to sessions.
354.q: Oh, a whole bunch of us who did recording sessions, finally got smart. I don’t know who thought of the idea, Don Lamond was a very busy drummer in those days, there was a guy who has since died, Terry Snyder who was doing the Como show. Very good drummer. Eddie Shaughnessy. Oh there were a whole…

897.t: Drummer with only a hi-hat on 'Give It Up'
897.s: White explains wanting a different sound without cymbals, which are musical tones that can clash and fill the space; the music has to breathe.
897.q: Yes. I wanted a certain sound. A lot of times I’m trying to get away from the generic common sound that you hear, and I had a certain sound in mind and I just kind of didn’t want, you know like a sock cymbal in that. Because the tendency is to, you know, give the back beat on the sock cymbal and I…

558.s: Stage by stage, conga and quinto in 1946, three congas in 1952, conga with bass drum and hi-hat in 1954, three congas with guiro, bell and singing in 1956.
558.q: Well, the first time was in 1946 when I came to the United States. That time I was playing the conga and the quinto because the pair of dancers that brought me were supposed to bring a conga player, and a bongo player to accompany their show. But as the budget was weak, they were like, "Well, the…

90.t: Roy Porter and the cymbal stand
90.s: Roy Porter replaces the older drummer and turns Edwards's music stand into a cymbal stand.
90.ch: Howard McGhee's band and bebop in LA
90.q: But anyway, back to Howard McGhee's thing, we had it going pretty good. And Monk was kind of an elder fellow. He was a nice drummer, but he just wasn't into this thing that we were doing. It was a little fast for him, you know. So while we were at the Downbeat, Howard brought in Roy Porter, and he…

381.t: Replacing a bass drum head every time a drunk punched through it
381.s: A patron broke his bass drum head each fortnight and paid $5; he soaked and tucked new calfskin heads by hand in a wash tub.
381.ch: Reel 4: boyhood bands and the drummers he admired
381.q: Well, there was a guy that used to come there every other Saturday -- he would come, and as soon as he would get drunk, the first thing he'd do was come up to the bandstand and knock a hole in my base drum. And I used to get so mad, but I had to smile because back in those days, you had better…

69.t: Tambourine and maracas in Duke's band
69.s: He played tambourine and sometimes maracas on Spanish pieces, the first percussion of that kind Duke's band had.
69.q: Well, I was playing the tambourine, the maracas sometimes, and some of my tunes and some matines -- you know, Spanish things like that.

70.t: Kaiser Marshall and the invention of the high-hat
70.s: Marshall was the first New York drummer with a high-hat; Jackson describes the earlier rat-trap foot cymbal Cuba Austin used.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: But I got to know Kaiser after I came to New York. He had left Fletcher but I still got to know him around New York because he still --

388.t: Zutty Singleton and the Shaw 'Blues' sides with the 25-inch cymbal
388.s: Leeman knew Zutty from 1936 and shows his influence on the Shaw 'A and B Blues' record, where he used the giant Chinese cymbal that sold out Bill Mather's shop.
388.q: Zutty and I were close and dear friends. I knew him from 1936 until his death in the '70's, which his work rubbed off on me and it influenced my work in that particular era, and it was especially predominant in the Artie Shaw record which was Blues A and Blues B, a collector's item now -- it was…

8.t: Old New Orleans drummers' limited kits and sounds
8.s: Old drummers had a snare, bass drum, side cymbal and wood blocks and made beats on the bass drum.
8.q: -- that's the next thing, they didn't have nothing but a set of drums. They had a drum and a snare drum and a bass drum and they had --

115.t: The sock cymbal and learning to play with both feet
115.s: Before the sock cymbal he used one foot; Abner Jones's bought pair of cymbals on sticks taught him to keep time with both feet.
115.q: And they started using it. Abner Jones, he had one that he bought, which was two pieces of stick with two cymbals on it, he'd keep offbeat with it.

124.t: Chick Webb's drum equipment: tympani heads, sticks, cymbals
124.s: Webb used xylophone and tympani, tympani heads on his drums, carefully chosen sticks and Zildjian cymbals, and pioneered the hi-hat.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: He used to use -- People wondered why his drums used to sound different from the other drummers. Well, Chick would use like on his drumhead, he would use like tympani heads.

103.t: Cuba Austin and how Jones came to the high sock cymbal
103.s: He explains that he raised the sock cymbal on a pipe and a coat hanger out of necessity after seeing Cuba Austin's low model.
103.q: He was with McKinney Cotton Pickers; and I saw him and he had this little sock cymbal that you used to slide your foot in. I have one at the shop. And by me running around like I said, all my friends never had what I had, the carnivals and circuses and what have you. It was through necessity that I…
